Markets

A tech and AI-chip rout pushed the S&P 500 into a correction yesterday, and the Nasdaq 100 had its worst week since 2020.

In brief: the S&P 500 fell about three and a half percent, the Nasdaq 100 about five and a half, small caps about three, and the Dow almost two. The news is that the VIX moved into the extreme bucket for the first time, closing near thirty-six. It is still in backwardation, now four sessions running. Implied volatility also still sits well above what the market has actually realized.

The first story is Nvidia. CNBC reports the stock plunged about fourteen percent, capping its longest weekly losing streak since 2008. MarketWatch says chip stocks lost two point three trillion dollars of value this week. Volume in Nvidia was about two and a half times normal. The damage spread. Broadcom fell about twelve percent, AMD about thirteen, Micron about fourteen, and Marvell about twelve. The tech sector fell more than seven percent and closed well below its recent highs.

Why the contagion? One explanation is that these stocks trade on one shared bet, which is that AI spending keeps growing. When the leader breaks, the market reprices the whole group, including its suppliers and customers. Positioning probably amplified it. Crowded winners get sold first when investors need to cut risk, and the selling feeds on itself. CNBC also reported that President Trump discussed Jensen Huang with Xi, and that Treasury Secretary Bessent said Nvidia chip export policy is unchanged. That is a reassurance, but it did not stop the selling. So the likely read is that this was less about one policy headline and more about a crowded trade unwinding. CNBC also notes that even Anthropic's blockbuster IPO could not escape the correction.

The second story is the odd behavior outside stocks. The ten-year yield fell about three percent to roughly four point nine percent. Normally falling yields help growth stocks, because their far-off profits are discounted at a lower rate. Not this time. Gold fell about four and a half percent to a new one-year low, and bitcoin fell about five percent, also to a one-year low. When safe havens and speculative assets drop together, one explanation is forced selling. Investors raise cash by selling whatever they can, not just what they want to sell. Yields falling is consistent with some money fleeing into Treasuries. The dollar barely moved. Consumer staples were the only sector to finish higher, up about two thirds of a percent, a classic defensive rotation.

Underneath, the damage was broad. Only about one hundred and twenty-four S&P 500 stocks rose, against about three hundred and seventy-six that fell. The share above their fifty-day average dropped to about forty-three percent from about seventy-two percent five days earlier. Goldman Sachs fell nearly seven percent on more than twice normal volume, and Intuit fell almost thirteen percent on three and a half times normal volume. Nothing in the news flow clearly explains that Intuit move. Yesterday was also monthly options expiration, which can add to late-day swings, but the size of this move points to something bigger than expiration mechanics.

The put to call ratio rose to about point seven seven from about point six two, so traders bought more protection.

Concept of the day: why index skew is steeper than single-stock skew. Index options are the market's main insurance product, so out-of-the-money index puts carry higher implied volatility than equally distant calls. That is the skew. With the VIX near thirty-six and the put to call ratio rising, that insurance demand is visible today. The options angle is that put spreads, which sell the further-out put, recover part of that rich premium while keeping the risk defined. What to watch for is the term structure returning to contango, which usually comes with put skew relaxing.
